name: Verbena

project_scope.note: B013 Verbena set. Brazilian vervain is retained as invasive comparison and excluded from native totals.

study_strategy.warning: Ignore flower color first; all five can look like generic purple-flowered vervains from a distance.

quick_key.if: slender plant + deeply pinnatifid lower leaves transitioning to narrow/simple upper leaves
low gray-green plant densely covered in whitish hairs
robust plant + broad harsh sandpaper leaves + very long slender spikes
very tall open candelabra-like plant + simple narrow serrate leaves + many short compact spikes

curation_status.photo_arrow_status: three new leaves annotated; matched hair macros and scabra/brazilian leaf close-ups pending
curation_status.visual_source_rights: verified four Wikimedia CC licenses; UT/USGS references link-only

look_here_first: Look at LEAVES and the whole flower-spike architecture before flower color. Broad rough leaves vs finely divided vs 3-lobed vs gray-hairy vs narrow unlobed are the fastest splits. Then compare whether spikes are long and slender or numerous, short and compact. Brazilian vervain is an introduced comparison, never a target-native recommendation.
shared_traits: Opposite leaves on often 4-angled stems; leaf shape varies dramatically among these five species.
Small flowers are arranged in elongated spikes or branched arrangements of spikes.
Fruit divides into four one-seeded nutlet-like mericarps.
Leaf outline, density/type of hairs, and spike architecture usually separate species faster than pale lavender-purple flower color.

species_comparison_matrix.first_trait: Lower leaves often deeply pinnatifid; upper leaves narrower and simpler

species_comparison_matrix.surface: Canescent, dusty-gray stem and leaf hairs

species_comparison_matrix.first_trait: Repeated deeply 3-lobed leaves, long central lobe
Broad, harshly scabrous or sandpapery leaves
species_comparison_matrix.spikes: Long slender spikes on a robust tall plant

species_comparison_matrix.first_trait: Tall airy, many-tiered branching canopy with narrow, unlobed serrate leaves
species_comparison_matrix.surface: Not broadly sandpapery like V. scabra
species_comparison_matrix.spikes: Many compact short terminal spikes in a candelabra-like panicle

comparison_cards.title: Texas vervain vs gray vervain
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Get a close side-by-side view of leaves. Texas vervain has a greener, more lightly hairy look and distinctly divided lower leaves. Gray vervain stays low and densely covered with grayish-white hairs.

field_matrix.halei: Lower leaves often strongly pinnatifid; upper leaves become narrow and simple
field_matrix.canescens: Narrow oblong to linear leaves, usually few teeth/short lobes
Dense pale hairs create an overall gray cast

comparison_cards.caution: Leaf division can vary within one plant; compare lower leaves at the same developmental stage.

comparison_cards.title: Texas vervain vs Gulf vervain
comparison_cards.look_here_first: Compare individual mature leaves from the lower-to-middle stem: slender, variable pinnatifid leaves on Texas vervain versus coarse, often regularly three-lobed leaves on Gulf vervain. Check hair texture, too.

field_matrix.halei: Variable, often pinnatifid lower leaf; narrow often simple upper leaves
field_matrix.xutha: Often prominently 3-lobed leaves with long center lobe
Coarse, hispid, sometimes glandular with pustulate bases
Coarser branching with terminal and axillary spikes

photo_pair_targets.arrow: hispid swollen hair bases versus fine sparse hairs

comparison_cards.caution: Do not use 'three-lobed' as a single absolute test because some V. halei leaves are also divided.

comparison_cards.title: Sandpaper vervain vs introduced Brazilian vervain
comparison_cards.look_here_first: First look at the leaves and spikes. Sandpaper vervain has broad, harsh-textured leaves and long thin spikes; Brazilian vervain has much narrower simple serrate leaves and many shorter compact spikes on tall airy branches.

field_matrix.brasiliensis: Numerous short, compact spikes in a widely branching panicle

photo_pair_targets.arrow: blade width + serrated edge + rough surface
long spikes versus compact candelabra tips
spike rachis length and flower density

comparison_cards.caution: Tiny lavender flowers occur on both; shape of individual flowers is not the primary field cue.

realistic_lookalikes.caution: Sometimes called prairie verbena and historically placed with Verbena; distinguish accepted genus and distinctly dissected/lobed leaf and flowering head architecture before labeling.
Small native verbena-like plant; include as a lookalike in cross-genus study, not a sixth Verbena card.
Non-native purpletop vervain with dense, showy rounded flowerheads; do not misidentify it as Brazilian vervain merely because both can be tall.

diagnostic_photo_checklist.needed: Matched lower mature leaves, same-scale hairs along leaf blade and rachis, whole-plant height
diagnostic_photo_checklist.status: flower/spike arrow coverage now present; matched leaf/stem hairs still pending

diagnostic_photo_checklist.needed: Same-scale three-lobed vs pinnatifid leaf photos, pustulate hair bases and mature upper leaves
Broad rough blade vs narrow simple leaf; tall inflorescence with long thin vs short compact spikes
Repeated middle-stem 3-lobed leaf vs nearly linear gray-hairy blades
Whole inflorescence and individual leaf close-ups; avoid genus confusion from common names

visual_comparison.title: Verbena leaf comparisons · real photographs
visual_comparison.subtitle: Leaves first, then hairs and inflorescence. These close-ups are real species-matched photos, with learner-added arrows placed only on visible parts.
visual_comparison.memory_rule: Halei: thin branched spikes · Canescens: dense short hairs · Xutha: coarse flowering axis + lobed foliage · Brasiliensis: many tiny compact heads. Flower color alone is a trap.

items.label: Texas vervain · deeply cut lower leaf
items.image_role: Mature leaf lobes, tapering blade base
items.creator: Larry Allain / U.S. Geological Survey
items.caption: Photo verifies deeply incised lateral lobes of one Texas vervain leaf. Some upper leaves are narrower and less divided; shape overlaps with Gulf vervain.

items.label: Gray vervain · foliage and habit
items.image_role: Narrow lobed leaves on a compact plant
items.creator: Gaiacoyote
items.caption: Field photograph shows narrow, toothed or incised foliage. It does NOT resolve the fine gray hairs; use separate UT macro for the canescence test.

items.label: Gulf vervain · opposite incised leaves
items.image_role: Flowering stem with incised opposite leaves
items.creator: Larry Allain / U.S. Geological Survey
items.caption: Whole flowering stem with a lower incised leaf visible to the left. Leaf is relatively small in frame; still need a proper three-lobed close-up for confident teaching.

items.label: Texas vervain · slender spike
items.image_role: elongated flowering spike with open flower spacing
items.creator: Annika Lindqvist
items.caption: Notice the slender flower spike and its spaced individual flowers. This view does NOT show the decisive lower-leaf shape; use the linked leaf references for that confirmation.

items.label: Gray vervain · short stiff hairs
items.creator: Alison Northup
items.caption: Look along the side of the central flower axis, just behind the open bloom. The short, stiff hairs are visible. For final separation from V. halei, a matching LEAF-and-STEM hair macro is still needed.

items.label: Gulf vervain · developing spike
items.image_role: single flowering spike, buds and floral bracts
items.creator: Wendy McCrady
items.caption: The spike is clear; note its bud-bearing upper portion and open flowers lower down. The repeatedly 3-lobed LEAVES are the better species distinction and are not visible in this view.

items.label: Introduced Brazilian vervain · compact heads
items.image_role: short terminal flower spikes on branched flowering stem
items.creator: NOZO
items.caption: Each short compact flowering tip sits on a branched inflorescence. Compare with the much longer, thinner spikes and broad coarse leaves of native V. scabra. Introduced; not a local native planting species.
